train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged, in particular, that the [NRP] authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in [LOCATION] was in breach of Articles 3 and 8. The applicant was represented by the Aire Centre, an NGO situated in [ LOCATION]. The Danish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant’s father decided to take her to take care of her grandmother who was ill. Her father was informed that his daughter had been recognised as a refugee in the country of origin. The application was sent to the Immigration Service on [DATE_TIME] because she had been absent for a short period of time. The applicant was able to return to the UK with her mother and siblings after her grandmother was taken care of by other family members. However, she was unable to leave the UK because she did not have a residence permit. The Immigration Service took the decision to issue a new permit for her to stay in the UK. The decision was made because she was in danger of losing her visa as a result of being out of the country too long. The applicant had not seen her mother for [DATE_TIME]. It had been the latter’s voluntary decision to send the applicant to [LOCATION]. She could still enjoy family life with her mother to the same extent as before. The applicant spoke [NRP], but could not read or write the language. She was very afraid and could not reside in her country of origin as there was unrest. It is disputed whether the [N RP] authorities were aware of this. The immigration service received a questionnaire from the applicant. It was partly filled out and stated, inter alia, that it had been her parents’ decision that she should leave. The applicant's parents did not apply for retention of [her] residence permit before she left, and neither she nor her parents contacted the immigration authorities during her stay abroad. The case was decided on the documents submitted, before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), without any parties being summoned. On [DATE_TIME] it found against the applicant. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-family re-entry. The applicant's sister had assisted her in answering the questionnaire. It is stated for the record that it was not [the applicant's] decision to leave [LOCATION] and stay away so long. The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the City Court’s decision. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention. It took into account that the applicant's parents had sent her voluntarily to [LOCATION] to live with family for an indefinite period. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on [DATE_TIME].

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41012/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested in Poland on suspicion of having committed several offences of fraud, forgery, perjury, uttering threats, robbery and kidnapping. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard by the President of the Fourth Section of the Court. The applicant was indicted before the Katowice District Court. The bill of indictment listed several charges of fraud, forgery, perjury, robbery and kidnapping. The court found that the evidence obtained in the case sufficiently supported the charges laid against him. It referred the case to thekatowice Regional Court. An appeal was lodged by the applicant. He maintains he was forced to testify, subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that the conditions of his detention were poor. The application for release was dismissed. He requested that his detention be replaced by another preventive measure. The judge agreed and extended his detention until [DATE_TIME]. Katowice District Court dismissed the applicant’s application for release or as an alternative the replacement of detention by more lenient preventive measures. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant lodged a complaint with the Katowice Court of Appeal under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The court examined only the applicant's complaint and dismissed it. The proceedings are still pending. The applicant is still in detention. The hearings scheduled for [Dates_TIME], [D dates_time] and [D Dates_Time] were adjourned. The hearing on the merits was held on [DATES_TIME]. Court of Appeal held that there were no delays for which the Regional Court could be held responsible. It noted that the court, when deciding on administrative and procedural matters, acted without delay. The Court of Appeal referred this part of the complaint to the Katowice Regional Court for consideration. The applicant had withdrawn his complaint on [DATE_TIME] about the length of the proceedings before the District Court. The court considered irrelevant the fact that at the material time the trial had not yet commenced. It held that the proceedings had been discontinued since the applicant withdrew his complaint. The application was dismissed and the appeal will be heard again later this month.

name: Mustafa Yalgın
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court. He also submitted that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATE_TIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his rights to a free hearing within a reasonable time and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The court sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. On appeal, the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court ofCassation (askeri yargıtay) and the file was transmitted to it. The case originated in an application (no. 31892/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. He also alleged that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. He was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Ankara Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. The public prosecutor accused the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. He further charged the applicant with having been involved in a number of crimes such as killings, attacks and bombings. The court sentenced the applicant under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. The Court of Cassation (yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and the file was transmitted to it. The applicant was conditionally released pending trial.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATE_TIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Chamber declared the application admissible. The application for permission to build on a playing field was made in 1998. The application was made on behalf of an environmental group set up by the first to third applicants. The applicants made submissions on just satisfaction to which the Government replied. The council gave outline planning permission for the college to build. The first applicant set up two stands at the entrance of the shopping mall in the Galleries, alerting the public to the likely loss of the open space and seeking signatures to present to the Council. The fourth applicant formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the college’s proposal and to persuade the Council not to grant the college permission to building on the field. Security guards would not let the first applicant or her assistants continue to collect signatures on any land or premises owned by [PERSON]. The applicants had to remove their stands and stop collecting signatures. The fourth applicant continued to try and reach the public by setting up stands by the roadside on public footpaths. The deadline for letters of representation to the Council regarding the building works was [DATE_TIME]. On [D date_TIME] the applicants submitted the 3,200 letters of Representation they had obtained. The application has now been withdrawn. The petition has been removed from the Internet and replaced with a new version of the petition with the same name. Sunderland Council ran a consultation campaign under the banner ‘Your Council, Your Choice’ It informed local residents of three leadership choices for the future of the Council. British Legion (collection for Armistice Day), various photographers (advertising and taking of photographs) and British Gas (staffed advertising display) were allowed to use the Galleries for this purpose. This was a statutory consultation exercise carried out under section 25 of the Local Government Act 2000, which required local authorities to draw up proposals for the operation of “executive arrangements” and consult local electors. Some 8,500 people were reported as having responded to the survey.

name: Filiz Uyan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7496/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant had been convicted of being a member of a terrorist organisation and sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. She was taken to a hospital, escorted by three male security officers (two gendarmes and a male prison guard) and one female prison guard, in order to undergo an ultrasound scan by a gynaecologist. The bottom of the consulting room windows was only 50 cm above floor level and the windows were unprotected. The male securityOfficers refused to leave the consultation room for security reasons. They stated that they would wait behind a folding screen. The applicant was examined by a doctor at a hospital in the city of İzmir. The doctor did not ask the male security officers to leave the room or remove the applicant’s handcuffs, as required by ethical rules. She was given a warning for professional misconduct. The public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the prison guard. The applicant objected and the Turkish Medical Association quashed that decision. On [DATE_TIME] the Karşıyaka Assize Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the doctor's warning. The proceedings against the male prison guard were dropped. The application for bail was rejected. The case was referred to the Turkish Court of Human Rights.

name: Koray Düzgören
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56827/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who is a journalist, distributed a leaflet concerning the conscientious objector Mr [PERSON], outside the Ankara State Security Court. The latter had been previously convicted and sentenced on account of this press release. The Court (Second Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court. Under Article 29 § 3, the Court decided to examine the merits of the application as well as its admissibility. Izmir Association of the Opponents of War: The responsibility for this conference rests exclusively with me. The case, which was brought before the Ankara Military Court of the Office of the Chief of Staff where I was allegedly accused of committing the crime of 'inciting others to evade military service', was concluded on [DATE_TIME]. ... The army, unable to deal with us through judicial methods, think that they can draw the opponents of war away from the public view. As to the papers given by the Recruitment Office...I am going to burn them right now before your eyes... I am not a soldier and I never will be. The court held that it had competence to deal with the case pursuant to the Constitution and domestic law. The court, relying on Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, affirmed that freedom of expression and the free dissemination of ideas was not an absolute right. Citing relevant articles of the Criminal Code, the court reasoned that the provisions under which the applicant was charged pursued the aim of eliminating threats to the unity of the country, national security and sovereignty. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. In its decision the court, referring to domestic law and the jurisprudence of the Court, held that the military courts had jurisdiction and competence to try the applicant. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant left [LOCATION] in order to avoid imprisonment. The judgment given by the General Staff Court was in accordance with the law. The applicant left the country to avoid imprisonment in order to escape prosecution. The application was rejected on the grounds that the applicant did not have the right to be in the country at the time of the decision. The decision was upheld on appeal and the applicant was released on bail. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal for review. The appeal was dismissed on appeal on October 30, 2013. The trial was adjourned until October 31, 2013, at 11.30am on October 31.

The applicant, who is a journalist, distributed a leaflet concerning the conscientious objector Mr [PERSON], outside the Ankara State Security Court. The latter had been previously convicted and sentenced on account of this press release. The Court (Second Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court, the alleged interference with the applicant's right to freedom of expression. "I am not a deserter; I am a 'conscientious objector', I neither intend to do military service nor desert. There is no reason to desert, because I defend the principle that people should exercise their right not to doMilitary service without having to go into hiding," he says. "I am aware that I will be summoned for military service, but until I am summoned, whenever that may be there will be no changes to my lifestyle," he adds. "They can find me here and take me by force. But I will resist to the end in the barracks, and I am underlining that IWill refuse to domilitary service in any shape or fashion" The applicant claimed that he was a defender of freedom of expression and challenged the independence and impartiality of the court. The court held that it had competence to deal with the case pursuant to the Constitution and domestic law and that there was no ruling of the European Court of Human Rights which had concluded that military courts were extraordinary courts. The applicant was sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and to a fine of 1,520,000 [NRP] Liras (TL) (approximately 3.5 Euros (EUR) at the time of the events) The court considered that, by distributing the leaflet containing the press release which led to the conviction, the applicant's actions were deliberate and that he had committed the offence knowingly and willingly. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant left [LOCATION] in order to avoid imprisonment. the judgment given by the General Staff Court was in accordance with the law. The applicant was found guilty of misconduct in public office. He was sentenced to two years in prison, suspended for one year, and fined £400. The judge ruled that the applicant's actions were not in breach of the law, and he was not convicted of any crime. The sentence was suspended for two years, and the fine was reduced to £350. The case was adjourned until the next hearing on November 6, 2014. The appeal was dismissed on November 7.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case was decided by the Court and handed to the European Court of Human rights. The decision was upheld on appeal. The applicant was cautioned pursuant to Article 3 of the Criminal Evidence (Northern Ireland) Order [DATE_TIME] (“the 1988 Order”). Unfamiliar with this new law, the applicant again requested a consultation with a lawyer and this request was refused. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions admitting to his involvement in the assembly and planting of the bomb. The applicant signed a lengthy statement which described in considerable detail his part in the conspiracy to plant and detonate the bomb in Belfast. The application was dismissed and the applicant was released from prison on bail. The applicant was charged with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The applicant applied under section 8 of [LOCATION] (Emergency Provisions) Act [DATE_TIME] (as amended) to have the admissions and statement made during questioning excluded on the basis of his alleged ill-treatment. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. A voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury) began and the applicant gave evidence as to his treatment, particularly by one team of two detectives. The trial judge rejected the application, admitted the applicant's admissions and statement into evidence and adjourned his detailed judgment in these respects. The applicant did not subsequently give evidence at the trial. However, the trial judge cautioned the applicant, pursuant to Article 4 of the 1988 Order, as regards adverse inferences which could be drawn from this failure to give evidence. The trial judge summarised the applicant’s evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. He noted, inter alia, that there were inconsistencies in the accounts of. ill- treatment given to the applicant to the doctor on [DATE_TIME] and his evidence at trial. He found it impossible to accept that the monitoring screens (which relayed pictures from cameras in the interview rooms to a central control room) had not been monitored. The judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court. He also found that detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant's appeal against his sentence was rejected. The Court of Appeal of [LOCATION] noted that the trial judge had had the great advantage of seeing the applicant give evidence. It noted that both an accused and the police officers involved can equally have an incentive to lie and that many facts are capable of being looked at in two or more ways, but they must be considered sensibly and realistically. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicants had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory.

train_texts: The case was brought before the Court on [DATE_TIME] by the European Commission of Human Rights. The purpose of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. The case originated in two applications lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) against [LOCATION] and [ LOCATION] The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [Date_TIME) and to the declaration whereby [LOCation] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art. 46) The hearing was held in public at [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on the appointed day. Immediately prior to its opening, the Court had held a preparatory meeting. There appeared before the Court: Sir [PERSON], Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr. [Person], Barrister-at-Law, Mr, [P PERSON], Advocate, Counsel, Mrs, Scottish Office, Advisers, Delegate, and applicants’ solicitors. The President of the Chamber directed that the oral proceedings should open on [DATE_TIME] (Rule 38). Shortly thereafter, the President was replaced as President by the Vice-President of the Court. The Court heard addresses by Mr. [PERSON] for the Government, by Sir [Person) for the Commission and by. Mr.  [PPerson] forthe applicants. The Court decided on [DATE_TIME], that the consideration of the case should continue without resumption of the oral proceedings (Rule 26) The Court held that the Government had lodged at the registry various documents the production of which the Registrar had previously requested on the instructions of the President of the Chamber. The Chamber, by unanimous decision, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50) The applicants are [NRP] citizens born in [Date_TIME] and [D date_TIME) respectively. The applicants’ complaints to the Commission in so far as relevant to the present proceedings all related to the period [DATE_TIME] when Mr. [PERSON] was subject to the ordinary prison regime at [LOCATION]. The facts surrounding those grievances are briefly set out in the following paragraphs. The applicants claim that they were unfairly treated by the Prison Service and that they should have been allowed to leave the prison without an escort. The Court finds that the applicants were entitled to be treated on the same terms and conditions as other prisoners. The decision to grant the application was made on the basis that the conditions of [ LOCATION] would be more beneficial to the applicant during the period leading to his eventual release. Mr. [PERSON]’s incoming and outgoing mail was controlled by the prison authorities in accordance with the normal practice followed at the prison (see paragraph 24 below) The applicants also asserted before the Commission that on occasions the prison censorship officer read out aloud in front of other inmates letters from Mrs [Person], laughing or making comments about their contents. However, Mr. [DATE_TIME] did not make any complaint to the Governor of the Prison or the Secretary of State regarding the manner in which his mail was read, in particular about its being read aloud. He was able to receive visits under close supervision in a crowded visiting hall, with the result that he was not able to see his wife. Mr. [PERSON] was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in [DATE_TIME]. He served his sentence in Perth Prisons until he was detained as a Category D prisoner (that is, the lowest security category) at [LOCATION]. He was moved to the Training for Freedom Host. He was given a special licence to do unescorted community work outside the prison, initially for [Date_TIME] and then for a week. He also complained through his Member of Parliament to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration (the Ombudsman - see paragraph 39 below) The Ombudsman stated that he could not uphold Mr. [person]’s complaints. ' applicant's father was seriously ill and unable to walk or travel. Petition indicated that his father had been “ill for a considerable period’, but not that he was dangerously ill, which would have made him eligible for compassionate leave. His request was therefore refused on [DATE_TIME].
